title: How do the primes show the common factors of two numbers?
description: Forty five and seventy five are written as primes, one above the other. Groups of primes that sit in both are multiplied, one is added, and the biggest is picked as the highest common factor. Keeko's doubt, that the bigger number is the highest common factor, is tested by dividing.
teaching_notes: One idea: a group of primes found in both factorisations multiplies to a common factor, and the highest one is the HCF. Watch for students who think the bigger of the two numbers is the HCF.

source: Find the common factors and the HCF of 45 and 75.
video_script.why: The child can write numbers as primes and now uses the primes of two numbers together to find their common factors.
video_script.substitution: A group of primes that sits in both factorisations multiplies to a common factor, and one is a common factor of every pair.
video_script.anchor: Forty five and seventy five written as primes, one above the other.
video_script.wrong_answer: the highest common factor is seventy five
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says the highest common factor is seventy five, the bigger number. But seventy five does not divide forty five, and a common factor is never bigger than the smaller number.
video_script.payoff_line: The highest common factor is fifteen.

final_answer.spoken: the common factors are one, three, five and fifteen, and the highest common factor is fifteen

maths_rules: Groups in both: 3, 5 and 3 x 5 = 15. Not in both: 3 x 3 (only in 45) and 5 x 5 (only in 75).
With 1, the common factors are 1, 3, 5, 15. The highest is 15 (45 / 15 = 3 and 75 / 15 = 5).
Slip: 75 is bigger than 45, so 75 cannot divide 45 and is not a common factor.
video_script.design: One idea: groups of primes found in both factorisations give the common factors. Assumes prime factorisation. Wrong idea: the bigger number is the HCF. The two factorisations stay on the board all video.
